items.title: HackerTube: YouTube built from videos recommended by HN
items.content:
It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with: hackertube.org !

Opus downloaded all comments of HackerNews, filtered them down, ran Sonnet over them in a workflow, got rid of spam and low grade content, and narrowed them down to just 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila!

This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5 <3.

items.title: An outsider's perspective on Scion and Mononoke
items.summary: vcs
items.content:
An outsider’s perspective on Scion and Mononoke

Recently, Anthropic wrote a blog post about their new centralized version control system Scion . As someone working on the Source Control team at Databricks, where we have a huge monorepo and are exploring different options, I figured it might be useful to share my perspective here.

(Obligatory disclaimer: This post represents my own views, not my employer’s.)

I recommend reading Anthropic’s post before continuing to read this one.

You may also want to pre-read Rain Paharia’s Anthropic’s Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke and the follow-up More on Anthropic’s Scion ripping off Mononoke .

Before we get into the weeds, it might be helpful to you to know where I’m coming from.

If you’re not interested in this, you can jump to the Technical Commentary section.

I have never worked at Facebook, but one of my all-time favorite tech talks is Durham Goode’s Scaling Mercurial at Facebook from Git Merge 2017. Goode was the longest-serving and most senior member on Facebook’s Source Control team. ( source )

The talk covers various interesting aspects for both the server side and the client side. For the server side, some of the topics include solving push contention with server-side rebasing (pushrebase), using scalable object storage for commits, moving various source control queries to the server, etc. For the client, there’s mention of the smartlog and other CLI commands for easier manipulation of history (compared to rebasing in Git).

However, more so than the technical aspects of the talk (which are interesting in their own right!), the main thing that has stayed with me throughout these years is the deep care for users that is reflected in Goode’s tone and words. It’s a bit difficult to convey this without the power of voice, You should watch the presentation!

but here are some quotes which reflect this:

In the context of hg smartlog : hg smartlog gives you a focused view of your branches and how they relate to the development trunk.

I know Git can produce this kind of UI if you know the incantation, but the critical thing here is not that it can be done; it’s that it becomes the default view of their source-control environment. That is where the power comes from: making it really intuitive for users to use source control and understand the concepts without reading a man page.

In the context of hg absorb : hg absorb auto-magically identifies the right commits in a stack to squash fixes into and rewrites history accordingly. This makes it easier to work with stacked changes.

This is the type of UI that we need to be inventing for our users: ones that match their intent and do it to the best of their ability, without making the user understand everything they have to do. It’s a little bit magic, but it’s magic in a very clean way. I think a lot of user experiences could benefit from this approach.

If you want to undo an amend or undo parts of a commit in Mercurial, you just run unamend and uncommit. You don’t have to understand a reflog; you don’t have to get a PhD to understand reset anymore. It just works, and it gives users confidence that they can recover from mistakes. That’s one of the most important things we can do: provide user experiences that give them confidence in what they’re doing.

On the user experience side, we as a source control community need to do a better job of building UIs that are accessible, intuitive, and that enable novice users to be power users. Everything I just talked about is how we are trying to do that for our users at Facebook. If the Git community could do that, the massive number of Git users taking advantage of it has the potential to redefine productivity for an entire generation of users.

Over the years, the possibility of these workflows lingered in my mind as I continued working with Git. I tried building my own wrappers on top of the git CLI to do some of these things, but I couldn’t get the performance to be reasonable…

items.title: Oh captain, our captain: Ars staff remembers Patrick Stewart
items.content:
Along with the rest of the world, we at Ars are mourning Sir Patrick Stewart —the beloved award-winning actor best known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men franchise—who died Wednesday at the age of 86.

A statement released by Stewart’s representatives said:

We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia. He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.

Through the actor’s X account , the family has requested that, in lieu of flowers, memorial contributions be made to the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center Fund and the Alzheimer’s Foundation of America Caregiver Resources .

Born in Yorkshire, England, in 1940, the acting bug bit Stewart at the age of 12, when his English teacher handed out scripts for Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice and asked young Patrick to read the part of Shylock—a role the adult Stewart would later play for the Royal Shakespeare Theater (RSC), among many other parts. His signature bald head emerged early, around 19, thanks to alopecia. He briefly worked as a cub reporter and a furniture salesman before winning a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theater School, and he landed his first professional role in 1959, playing a marooned pirate in a production of Treasure Island for the Lincoln Repertory Company.

Stewart worked regularly in theater and on British television, and his big break came in his late 40s. The actor was conducting master classes on Shakespeare at the University of California, Los Angeles, when a TV producer developing TNG  heard him lecture and thought he would make a perfect captain for the Enterprise-D . Creator Gene Roddenberry wasn’t initially keen on the choice, but Stewart’s audition changed his mind. The rest is television history.

On Instagram , fellow thespian Sir Ian McKellen—who first met Stewart when both were young actors with the RSC and co-starred as Magneto in the X-Men films—recalled the day Stewart told him about the Star Trek offer.

“’But Patrick, think of your stage career in the UK,'” McKellen recalled saying. “‘Do you really want to risk—getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?’ Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did.”

Stewart himself never expressed anything but pride in the role. “For huge numbers of people, I will always be Jean-Luc Picard, and that’s fine,” he told The Independent in 2003. “I really believe we created an admirable individual.”

TNG ended in 1994, but it wasn’t long before Stewart created another iconic role, starring as Professor Charles Xavier in 2000’s  X-Men , alongside McKellen as Magneto. He reprised the role in six more films and voiced the character in multiple video games.

He was a serious actor who never took himself too seriously, relishing Shakespeare, Ibsen, and Beckett but also throwing himself into comedic TV appearances on Saturday Night Live, The Daily Show (he was a “special correspondent” for several segments in 2012), and Sesame Street . Who could forget his timeless “Soliloquy on B,” channeling Hamlet? Or his daily readings of Shakespearean sonnets that helped us all get through the COVID-19 pandemic? He voiced Napoleon in 1999’s Animal Farm , CIA Deputy Director Avery Bullock on American Dad and, earlier this year, Sir Nitchfield in the delightful Sheep Detectives .

In between acting gigs, Stewart found time for charity work, advocating for such causes as domestic violence prevention and PTSD awareness among members of the armed forces,…

온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-117518 📢 Source: openjs 💣 CVSS Score: 8.2 (HIGH) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False @fastify/reply-from is a Fastify plugin that forwards requests to an upstream HTTP server. In versions up to and including 12.8.0, the plugin validated proxy paths against forward-slash dot-segments only and then built the target with the WHATWG URL parser, which normalizes a backslash and its percent-encoded form to a forward slash on the http, https, ws, and wss schemes. A path that uses backslash dot-segments therefore bypasses the traversal check and resolves to a different upstream path, so an application that scopes proxying to an upstream prefix, or relies on route guards in front of the forwarding call, can have an unauthenticated request escape the intended prefix and reach other upstream endpoints. The resulting access to unintended upstream resources is primarily a confidentiality impact with limited integrity impact. The issue is fixed in @fastify/reply-from 12.8.1, where the path is normalized and any segment resolving to a single or double dot, along with control characters and ambiguous whitespace, is rejected before the URL is constructed, and users should upgrade to 12.8.1 or later. There is no workaround other than upgrading. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-02T10:39:22.468Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-117518

items.summary_ko: @fastify/reply-from 12.8.0 이하 버전에서 경로 검증을 우회하는 취약점(CVE-2026-117518)이 확인되었다. 백슬래시를 이용한 dot-segment 경로가 탐색 방지 검사를 통과해 의도하지 않은 업스트림 경로로 연결될 수 있으며, 인증되지 않은 요청이 지정된 접두사 밖의 엔드포인트에 접근할 수 있다. 주로 기밀성에 영향을 주며 CVSS 점수는 8.2(HIGH)이고, 12.8.1 버전에서 수정되었으므로 업그레이드가 권장된다.

items.title: Tyrtulia, a headless forum with no passwords, made for the terminal
items.summary: linux, python, show
items.content:
I like forums. Debates, questions, answers, opinions, etc. That feeling of an asynchronous community, where answers are thought through and content lasts, is what makes the internet an interesting place. That is why I like reading them and taking part in them. But I had never designed or built one. In my spare time I started sketching one, and I ended up building my humble headless , federated forum, with simple, modern technologies and open standards.

And I learned a lot along the way. A forum looks simple, but it hides the classic problems of any server. Who can do what? How do you tell a moderator from a regular user? What happens when you have to ban someone? How do you stop someone from stealing an account? Roles, permissions, bans and security. I had to solve them one by one, and you don't learn that by reading.

The server only offers a solid, documented API. It is REST with hypermedia: the client only knows one route, GET / , and discovers everything else by following links. Underneath there are some very boring standards:

RFC 9110: HTTP semantics, with ETag and If-Match so edits don't overwrite each other.

There is no web interface, no forms, no advanced authentication systems, no file handling (images, attachments, etc.), and nothing that isn't strictly needed to read and write messages.

That is why it is so light. It uses between 60 and 70 MB of RAM and about 50 MB of disk. It only needs Python and SQLite to run.

How does a client know what it can do? The server tells it with links. Look at the same request, GET / , made by a guest (simplified):

"latest": {"href": "/threads", "method": "GET"},

"search": {"href": "/search{?q,author,in}", "method": "GET", "templated": true},

"login": {"href": "/sessions", "method": "POST", "schema": "/schemas/session"}

"latest": {"href": "/threads", "method": "GET"},

"search": {"href": "/search{?q,author,in}", "method": "GET", "templated": true},

"createThread": {"href": "/threads", "method": "POST", "schema": "/schemas/thread"},

"notifications": {"href": "/notifications", "method": "GET"},

"events": {"href": "/events", "method": "GET", "type": "text/event-stream"}

If I change a route tomorrow, no client breaks, because none of them knew it in advance. They just follow the links the server gives them.

I know there are very complete free software forums:

NodeBB : Node.js, with MongoDB, Redis or PostgreSQL. It stands out for real time with WebSockets.

They are all fantastic, but they are designed to be used from a web browser. They also have an ambitious scope. That is ideal for large communities, but too much for a small, light forum.

That said, Tyrtulia doesn't give up on the browser: it can be indexed by search engines and anyone can read it on the web.

No OAuth, no OpenID, no sign-up forms. There are two ways to authenticate:

Your Unix user : the client talks to the forum through a Unix socket. The operating system tells the forum which user is on the other side. No sign-up, no login. Your user is your account.

SSH key : the client connects over HTTP and the forum sends it a challenge. The client signs it with your private SSH key and the forum verifies it with your public key.

There is no registration over HTTP. If you have a Unix user on the server, you already have an account: it is created the first time you connect through the socket. From there you can add your SSH keys to log in from outside. If you don't have a user on the machine, the administrator creates an account for you with your public key from the command line. On a tilde, having a Unix user is already the invitation.

Easy to use, secure, and no passwords to steal.

The idea isn't mine. I was inspired by BBJ , a bulletin board for the terminal built for small communities or clubs (tildes, pubnixes, club servers, etc.). I took its spirit and brought it to my own ground. Still, there are important differences.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Microsoft Patents an AI That Can Literally Put Words in People’s Mouths in Real Time: Talk about a new kind of filter.
items.content:
Microsoft just filed a patent for an AI product that would be able to transform live video in real time to alter speakers’ words and faces.

The patent, as first flagged by patent-tracker Patentlyze , is described by its inventors as a “near real-time artificial intelligence (AI) enhancement of video or augmented reality (AR) presentations of live events.”

Using AI agents, the system would identify and alter or remove certain words, while editing a speaker’s face and mouth to match. The agents would rely on set parameters or user profiles to make the changes, and would also edit the video and audio just before and after a removed or replaced word to allow for “smooth transitions.”

In an era of media and the internet increasingly defined by AI-fueled deepfakes, disinformation, and information-muddling slop, the system described in this patent may represent a new world of filtering tools that subtly alter reality as it takes place, in this case on a highly-personalized level. Viewers, the patent suggests, could consume whatever live event they want to without hearing what they don’t want to hear.

The potential use cases floated in the patent vary. One possible application is real-time translation, with the system allowing for broadcasts and other live footage to be both heard and seen in a viewer’s preferred language.

The patent also posits that such a tool could be used to remove filler words like “um” or “ah” from live speech, or to erase stutters or speech impediments.

Other possible use cases, though, go much further. According to the patent, the system could be used to cut down on “personal words or phrases” like “coined terms,” as well as “colloquial terms” like the term “y’all” or the phrase “bite the bullet.” The patent also claims that the system could eliminate “mumbled words, mispronounced words, misused words, misspoken words, offensive words, insensitive words, or inappropriate words.” Replacement words, it adds, may come from an “internet search.”

In other words, live broadcasts may not be so live anymore after all.

Microsoft didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Dubbing has existed for ages, and video footage is edited all the time, both for normal and for insidious reasons. Automatically editing live videos in this way with the help of AI agents, however, could change how audiences fundamentally engage with live footage. As it stands, if people don’t like what they hear, they can simply turn something off; the system outlined by Microsoft describes an environment where people can instead adjust someone else’s speech to their personal taste. Language translation aside, does using a tool that eliminates errors, or erases words and phrases associated with a speaker’s local dialect, move us further into personalized bubbles? What’s so bad about hearing someone from the South say “y’all?”

To that end, the patent does mention that an event’s original live video and audio may be recorded and stored for the sake of “ground truth,” nodding to potential misuse and confusion that could arise from such a tool.

The kinds of live footage that could be transformed by the system include lectures, presentations, a range of television productions — awards ceremonies, game and cooking shows — and live sports, among several others.

items.title: hi @brendt
items.content:
PHP had one of the biggest security incidents in history two weeks ago. Of course, it's only guessing how many websites didn't bother to update, and we're likely only see the effect of those websites potentially being hacked months or years from now. Active PHP professionals were of course quick to upgrade, and soon the dust settled.

But yes, I am conflicted. Not because of the zombie websites out there — there's no saving them anyway — but because of the countless PHP projects running unsupported versions; anything lower than 8.2. This would have been the perfect moment to put in the work to get back up to date (and stay up to date for the years to come).

And that's what PHP itself is pushing for: they only make security releases for recent versions. However, soon after the patches were released, Ondřej Surý was able to backport them to older, unsupported versions; making it so that outdated projects could still benefit from the security release.

That in itself isn't a bad, by the way. I'm glad there were backports available so quickly, making sure as little websites as possible would be vulnerable to these newly discovered security issues.

But… it's not really a long-term solution; is it? This whole ordeal depended on one person deciding to backport security patches. That's a major bottleneck. On top of it, it gives a false sense of security to anyone running unsupported PHP versions. What will happen the next time a critical vulnerability is discovered? Will Ondřej be there again? What about the time after that one? And after that one?

You could argue that this would be a better job for the Foundation to take care of? And I would say: they already do! They support up to four years of PHP releases, that is plenty of time for any project to upgrade to the latest version. Even more so in this day and age of AI: getting your projects up-to-date has never been as trivial as it used to be.

But no, instead we've applied a band-aid to one wound, hoping by the time the next one comes around, Ondřej will be there once again.

What I want to say… Just update. Just do it. Do it now without time pressure, instead of postponing until the next time a critical vulnerability is disclosed right when you're on vacation or having a day off.

Invest in certainty instead of gambling.

items.title: 대기업 총수, 의장 경제문제 때문에 못조져 놓는다는 건
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

items.title: An Italian farmer found some unknown seeds in his attic and planted them
items.content:
At his farm near Parma, Italy, Claudio Grossi offers a visual history of his miracle grain in photos, crackers and loaves.

Sometime in the early 1990s, Claudio Grossi, a 40-year-old farmer in Parma, in northern Italy, was cleaning his attic when he turned up an old sack full of seeds that he couldn’t identify. The bag, he was sure, had been left by his late great-grandfather, who’d started the farmstead around 1915. Grossi had no idea how long the seeds had been sitting there, deprived of water, soil and sun. Dry and cracked, the kernels looked so old in the palm of his hand that he doubted anything would ever sprout from them. He carried the bag down the stairs, shook the seeds out into a pile of manure and then forgot about them.

To his surprise, the seeds soon sprouted a few different types of wheat. One was particularly striking: At six feet high, its plants were about twice as tall as commercial wheat. But the most remarkable feature came when it developed ears—the grain-studded parts at the top of the plant. All of the wheat types Grossi had previously seen grew only one such ear. But the tall wheat grew a full seven ears, always in the same pattern: a long one with six shorties bunched up around it like little fingers. Even the kernels themselves were bigger than those of average wheat. And unlike the typical pale-yellow wheat kernels, they came in a rainbow of colors—yellow, black, red, white and even green, sometimes all on the same stem. Grossi, a grain farmer his whole life, had never seen anything like it. “I thought it was a freak of nature,” he says. He couldn’t find a mention of it in agricultural books.

Ears grown from the very first seeds Grossi discovered in his attic. Grossi prizes these first grains, now preserved under glass in his kitchen.

This article is a selection from the November 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine

For Grossi, a practicing Catholic, the next insight came from a different book altogether. Leafing through a Bible at church one Sunday, he found a passage in the Book of Genesis describing a stalk with seven ears, in a dream that Joseph interprets for the Pharaoh: “And he slept and dreamed the second time: And, behold, seven ears of grain came up upon one stalk, rank and good. And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them. And the seven thin ears devoured the seven rank and full ears.” To Grossi, that sounded just like the mysterious crop in his manure pile.

“I connected the dots,” Grossi says. That grain must be really ancient , he thought. And if people were farming this odd-looking wheat in biblical times, why does no one today?

Back on his farm, Grossi harvested the grain, milled it into flour and baked a loaf of bread in his kitchen. Compared with commercial wheat, the dough didn’t rise well, but as the loaf sat in the oven, it filled the kitchen with a surprisingly nutty and delicious aroma. Once finished, it had a rich, satisfying taste. “You get these notes of sweetness that you can’t find in regular commercial flour,” he says.

Did you know? More miracles of grain in the Bible

In 2 Kings 4:42-44 , Elisha multiplies 20 barley loaves in order to feed 100 men—anticipating Jesus’s “Feeding of the 5,000” in the gospels.

In 1 Kings 17:8-16 , Elisha helps a widow at Zarephath to outlast a drought and famine with only a handful of flour and a little oil.

In Judges 7:9-15 , a Midianite soldier recounts a dream in which a barley loaf tumbles into the camp and overturns a tent. Gideon, the judge and military leader, recognizes the dream as a sign that God will deliver the Midianites into Israel's hands.

In 2 Kings 4:38-41 , during a famine, someone gathers wild gourds and cuts them into a pot of stew. The diners discover that the stew is dangerous and cry out to Elisha. He calls for flour and throws it into the pot—and the stew becomes miraculously safe to eat.

items.title: Postgres 19 is late, and it's AI's fault
items.summary: databases, practices
items.content:
Over the past decade, the timing of PostgreSQL major releases has become very predictable: no earlier than the middle of September, and no later than the middle of October. This year is going to be different. PostgreSQL 19 most likely won’t be released until November, and it’s not impossible that the project could decide to postpone the release further.

Moreover, this year, several rather large features were reverted quite late in the beta period: UPDATE/DELETE FOR PORTION OF , SQL Property Graph Queries (SQL/PGQ), and ALTER TABLE … MERGE PARTITION/SPLIT PARTITION were all reverted between August 27 and September 15. While major feature reverts are not especially uncommon immediately after feature freeze, which each year occurs on April 8, it is unusual to see multiple major features get pulled from the release at such a late date. So, what happened?

The short answer is that LLMs happened. All software contains bugs, and PostgreSQL’s code base is large, complex, and old. Our git history – converted from CVS – now reaches back more than 30 years, and the first code was written a decade before that. There’s a huge amount of code, and that code contains a huge number of bugs. That’s always been true, and it hasn’t stopped PostgreSQL from being popular or successful. What’s different now is that it’s become vastly easier to find those bugs. Fixing them has also gotten easier, but not to the same degree.

Between April 8th, 2025 and September 25, 2025, there were 1037 commits to PostgreSQL’s master branch and 724 commits to REL_18_STABLE . In 2026, during the same date range, there were 1443 commits to the master branch and 1169 commits to REL_19_STABLE . In other words, if you look at the number of commits that went into the master branch only between feature freeze and September 25th, it actually declined slightly from last year to this year, but the number of back-patched commits jumped by more than 60%.

It’s possible that some of this jump is the result of committers making more mistakes this year than they did last year, but I don’t think anyone who works on the project really believes that’s the main cause. Rather, it seems likely that PostgreSQL committers were about as conservative in 2026 as they were in preceding years, but a lot more of the mistakes they made were quickly found by LLMs.

And it isn’t just mistakes in the latest release. In the same time period, during 2025, there were 248 commits to REL_17_STABLE , and during 2026, there were 433 commits to REL_18_STABLE . In other words, the number of commits being back-patched not just to the release in progress but also to at least one prior release jumped by more than 74% in a single year. The reason for this is simply that a huge number of people on the Internet are now reporting bugs in PostgreSQL that they found using LLMs, and the PostgreSQL committers have been very, very busy fixing them.

And I think that’s also why we had so many late reverts, and why the release itself is delayed. Two factors are at play here.

First, because so many more bugs are being found now, it takes more time to fix them. LLMs can draft fixes, but those fixes aren’t always correct or compliant with PostgreSQL standards. So, they still need to be reviewed and committed by humans, and those humans have not gotten any smarter between 2025 and 2026.

Second, time that would have been spent reviewing what went into the release got diverted into addressing security issues and other bugs in the back-branches, and so it took longer to figure out what needed to be reverted before shipping v19.

In the end, I don’t think that the delay in shipping PostgreSQL 19 is particularly concerning. It is not a long delay in the grand scheme of things, and it emerges directly from the project’s concern for quality.

items.title: French lawmakers add $11.2 billion internet tax based on traffic usage to budget, costs $0.06 per gigabyte of content accessed — law still has to pass Senate approval.
items.content:
Edit 11/1/2026 4:25am PT: Clarified title to state the bill still has to pass the Senate after being added to the budget.

France has approved a proposed tax that aims to tax the amount of internet data per gigabyte sent to French users in the country, with major companies like Google , Netflix, TikTok, and Meta now in the crosshairs. According to minutes released by the National Assembly, members voted 11-10 in support of the motion on October 30 — which now means the new law has been added to the country’s next budget, despite major opposition from the government side and the finance committee rapporteur. The law still has to pass through the Senate for final approval. The latest amendment, introduced by socialist lawmaker Laurent Lhardit, could see content providers pay €0.055 (roughly $0.06) to the government for every gigabyte of content distributed to French users.

With approximately 154 million users and counting in France, the proposal’s authors say such a tax could generate around €10 billion ($11.2 billion) in annual revenue for the government. “This amendment proposes a tax on digital data flows emitted by content providers, to be borne by the providers themselves. Its revenue is estimated at €10 billion.” Said Laurent Lhardit. The said proposal, though yet to be passed as it must survive further parliamentary scrutiny, aims at companies that generate substantial internet traffic as opposed to taxing their advertising revenue, profits and subscriptions. Its explanatory notes particularly mention Google , Meta, Netflix, Amazon , and content delivery network Akamai as major potential contributors. Notably, TikTok and other similar platforms could fall under this broader scope depending on how these rules are applied.

Internet service providers, including Orange Free and Liad, would be required to measure the volume of data and identify the companies responsible for sending it to French users. The Data will then be collected and submitted quarterly to France’s tax administration under the supervision of telecommunications watchdog Arcep. Aside from the €0.055 per gigabyte levy, the proposal also includes a cap of 15% of a company’s French revenue or 2% of its worldwide revenue. It also accounts for content delivery networks (CDNs), which store copies of online content closer to users to reduce loading times and network congestion.

Approximately 200 billion GB of data pass through French internet providers annually, with about five major companies identified in the amendment accounting for about half of that traffic. Lhardit argued that tax would primarily affect global technology companies because they generate most of the data traffic reaching French subscribers. He also disputed that those platforms would merely push additional costs to users, using Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok, which provide free access, as examples. “The rapporteur keeps arguing that the taxes will be passed on to consumers. However, I fail to see how a tax can be passed on to users of Facebook, Instagram, or TikTok since these services are free,” He stated.

How much money are you willing to spend during the Black Friday sales?

Lawmakers opposed to the proposal, however, argue that it is likely to endanger user privacy. Government Minister David Amiel questioned whether the internet traffic could be measured and attributed to content providers without introducing complicated monitoring requirements. Those concerns extend to potential consequences for French business. Lhardit, however, noted that businesses would pay relatively modest costs, citing TF1 as an example, which requires broadcasters to contribute between €200,000 and €300,000.

Several European countries already impose digital service taxes, generally based on revenue from Ads, marketplaces and other digital activities. items.title: 도청 당하는것같은데 어떡하죠 ㅠ
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

제가 집에서 한 말이나 제 언니랑 한 말들을 학교 가면 다 알고있어요 그래서 제가 말한 내용이랑 똑같은 내용을 꼭 제가 들을 수 있을때 언급하고 남자애들 여자애들 할것없이 제가 안보이는 데에서 조금만 이상한 말 하면 비웃으면서 지나가요 ㅠ 제가 진짜 친구가 없어서 학교에서 한마디도 안하는 날들이 대부분인데 제가 언니랑 학교 구석에서 말한 내용이랑 집에서 혼잣말 한 내용들을 똑같이 언급한게 한두번이 아니에요 ㅠ 제가 그냥 내용만 겹치면 말을 않겠는데 제가 말했던 내용 언급하면서 꼭 제 이름도 한번씩 부르고 그래요 보통 사람들은 자기이름을 그렇게 말하면 기분나빠서 한번 돌아보기라도 하겠지만 저는 성격이 워낙 내성적이라 누가 비웃고 지나가거나 째려보거나 저 보면서 한숨쉬어도 아무말도 못하거든요 ㅠ 그래서 그냥 기분만 나쁜건데 이게 하루이틀 쌓이니까 너무 힘들더라고요 ㅠ 처음엔 저도 이게 정신이 약간 아픈건가 했는데 정신병 관련 영상도 다 보고 그랬는데 환청은 이런식으로 들리는게 아니라고 하더라고요 계속 날 비난하고 그런식으로 들리는건데 저는 그런게 전혀 아니라 제가 전날 했던 얘기들, 방금 쉬는시간에 학교 구석에서 나눈 얘기들을 자꾸 똑같이 언급하니까 미치겠어요 ㅠ 한두번 우연으로 겹치는게 아니라 계속 겹쳐요 진짜.. 그리고 애초에 제가 학교에서 말을 한마디도 안하는데 자꾸 저한테 그런 반응을 보인다는게 애초에 저한테 이상한 일이 일어난다는 반증 아닌가요? 그리고 걔네가 말했던걸 몇개를 말씀드려보면 제가 도청을 의심한 초기에 급식실에서 밥먹고있었는데 어떤 남자애가 “도청” 이러고 지나가는거에요 그리고 저희반 남자애가 제 언니 이동수업반이랑 같은 반인데 거기서 쉬는시간에 “도청기를 달고다녀 ㅋㅋㅋㅋ” 이랬다는거에요 진짜 이상하죠 저는 예전에 우울증 약을 먹은적이 있어서 정신이 막 무결점으로 건강한 편은 아니에요 근데 저희 언니는 그런적도 없고 교우관계도 좋고 진짜 정신이 건강하거든요 ㅠ 근데 저희 언니가 그런말을 들었다니깐 진짜 도청이 일어나는게 맞는거구나 생각했어요.. 그리고 또 있었던 일을 말씀드리면 이동수업 때 제 뒷쪽에서 남자애가 제 아버지 직업을 언급하면서 제 이름을 말하는거에요 이게 도청을 하지 않고서는 절대 알수가 없는 사실이거든요 ㅠ 또 “정신병ㅋㅋㅋ” 하면서 제 이름을 언급하는거에요 이것도 도청을 하지 않았다면 알수 없는거고요 더 말씀드릴 사례가 많은데 그러면 너무 길어져서 이정도만 말씀드릴게요 그래서 찾아보니까 머리에 붙일수 있는 초소형 도청기가 있다길래  제 언니가 제 머리를 샅샅이 뒤져줬거든요? 근데 그래도 아무것도 안나오더라고요 ㅠ 그리고 또 도청 탐지 업체를 알아보니까 금액이 너무 비싸서요 ㅠ 제가 고3인데 이런일을 당해서 너무 스트레스 받는데 방법이 없어서 정말 어떻게 해야될지 모르겠어요 안그래도 제가 여자애들이나 남자애들이 괴롭힐 소재가 많은 조용한 애거든요 ㅠ그래서 저를 지나칠때 꼭 한마디 끼얹고 지나가고 그래서 학교생활이 막 편한 그런애는 아닌데 학교에서 유일하게 맘놓고 말할 수 있는 언니랑 말하는 얘기를 다 알고있으니까 스트레스 받아서 공부 능력도 점점 떨어지는것같고 쨋든 걱정이 이만저만이 아니에요 어떡해야되죠 ㅠㅠ 제가 성격이 활발한 편도 아니고 집에 돈이 많지도 않아서 진짜 대학 잘가야되는데 걱정이에요ㅠㅠ 긴글 읽어주셔서 감사하고요 여기가 사생활 침해 관련한 갤러리니까 혹여나 저랑 비슷한 경험이 있으시거나 관련 지식이 있는 분은 제가 어떻게 해야하는건지 알려주시면 진짜진짜 감사드릴것같아요 많은 도움 부탁드려요 정말 방법 여러가지 찾아봐도 안되겠어서 여기다 글 남겨요

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-117531 📢 Source: openjs 💣 CVSS Score: 5.9 (MEDIUM) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False @fastify/multipart is the multipart form-data and file upload plugin for the Fastify web framework. In versions 5.3.0 through 10.1.6, the plugin does not propagate a parser error to the file stream when a request body ends inside a file part with no closing boundary, even though the Content-Length is complete, the client does not abort, and no file size limit is exceeded. The plugin destroys the in-progress file stream without an error, so a handler that iterates the request parts and performs asynchronous work before consuming the file attaches to a stream that never emits an error or end event, and the request never responds while the connection stays open. An unauthenticated remote client can repeat these malformed uploads against such a route to accumulate pending connections and exhaust server resources, so the impact is availability only and exploitation depends on the application using a delayed file consumer. The issue is fixed in @fastify/multipart 10.1.7, where the parser error is propagated to the file stream so a delayed consumer settles with an error instead of hanging, and users should upgrade to 10.1.7 or later. There is no workaround other than upgrading. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-02T10:32:38.867Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-117531

items.content_ko: @fastify/multipart는 Fastify 웹 프레임워크용 multipart 폼 데이터 및 파일 업로드 플러그인이다. 5.3.0부터 10.1.6까지의 버전은 요청 본문이 닫는 경계 없이 파일 파트 안에서 끝나면 파서 오류를 파일 스트림에 전달하지 않는다. 이때 Content-Length는 완전하고 클라이언트는 연결을 끊지 않았으며 파일 크기 제한도 초과하지 않은 상태다. 플러그인은 진행 중인 파일 스트림을 오류 없이 파기하므로, 파일을 소비하기 전에 비동기 작업을 수행하는 핸들러는 오류도 종료 이벤트도 받지 못해 응답하지 않는다. 인증되지 않은 원격 클라이언트가 이런 잘못된 업로드를 반복해 대기 연결을 쌓으면 서버 자원이 고갈될 수 있으며, 영향은 가용성에 한정된다. 10.1.7에서는 파서 오류를 파일 스트림에 전달해 지연 처리 핸들러가 멈추지 않고 오류로 종료되도록 수정되었다. 본문은 사용자 조치 안내 부분에서 끊겨 있다.

items.title: Pratt parsing is a black box
items.summary: compilers, plt
items.content:
It caught my attention that most of Pratt parsing tutorials that I've stumbled on spend almost all of their time explaining Pratt's algorithm and none explaining the properties behind Pratt that actually matter. Pratt fits into just 9 lines of code if you're programming in a high-level language such as Rhombus:

And here's a secret: that's the least important thing you need to understand about Pratt's. In fact, you don't need to understand this piece at all! Imagine if you were only able to use quicksort if you understood its implementation. Imagine if you were only able to use files if you knew how to implement a filesystem from scratch. It's the same logic here. If you lack the power to abstract, you'll arrive nowhere in computer science because that's how the whole field works. In fact, I wrote the backbone of a heavily Pratt-based parsing machinery for a compiler that I've been writing since last year w/o even bothering to understand the above snippet in any detail.

Not convinced? Think for a second on how they do in traditional parsing techniques: compiler compilers! They use code generators to spit the parsing algorithm because just a minuscule crowd bothers to learn what the parsing engine is actually doing. It's no different with Pratt. However Pratt is so small that you can just copy'n'paste these 9 lines of code in your project and call it a day instead of adding a new complex dependency to your project. The algorithm hasn't changed since 1973 and it's not gonna change now.

In this article I'll go over what you actually need to keep in mind for Pratt parsing. The point won't be about memorizing any of it though. The point is about acquiring a mindset. As long as you acquire the mindset you don't need to even bother to remember even a single word of what I say here.

The only tutorial on Pratt parsing that I can firmly recommend to someone who has never been exposed to the topic is actually a talk that Douglas Crockford gave in the conference GOTO 2013 ¹ . Douglas Crockford nailed it when he stated:

Pratt takes parsing which is a really complicated thing and reduces it to one simple question: What do we expect to see to the left of a token ?

At first glance it may look like a mystical statement devoid of meaning, but that's the question that becomes the framework on how you face parsing problems and it'll rewire your brain to internalize the Pratt parsing mindset. That's the most important thing you need to understand. You register semantic actions for two categories: nuds and leds. A nud is a token that expects nothing to its left (nud stands for null denotation) while a led expects something (led stands for left denotation).

Traditional parsing techniques register semantic actions to production rules. Here's an example I took straight from GNU Bison's manual:

The text between the braces is code that executes when the BNF-like grammar on the left matches. I'm gonna repeat myself because that's really important: traditional parsing techniques register semantic actions to production rules (which by definition are non-terminal symbols). In contrast Pratt parsing registers semantic actions to the terminals themselves instead. That's a fundamental shift on how you face parsing problems.

Here's a stripped down version of the code for the tables that I have in my compiler right now:

rule_c < token :: lparen , token :: nud :: parse_lparen > ,

rule_c < token :: lbrace , token :: nud :: parse_lbrace > ,

rule_c < token :: code :: exclamation_mark , token :: nud :: parse_negation > ,

rule_c < token :: code :: less_than_sign , token :: nud :: parse_enter_type_scope > ,

rule_c < token :: code :: plus_sign , token :: nud :: parse_unary_plus > ,

rule_c < token :: code :: minus_sign , token :: nud :: parse_unary_minus > ,

rule_c < token :: code :: dplus_sign , token :: nud :: parse_preincrement > ,

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: ‘Wake Up Call:’ Fanfiction Writers and Readers React to AO3 Outage
items.content:
In the wake of fanfiction repository Archive of Our Own (AO3) announcing a weeks-long security incident outage, readers and writers are reflecting on why the site is important to the fanfiction community, and how they’re coping with the downtime.

On Thursday , the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the non-profit organization that runs AO3, posted that the site was down for maintenance, eventually updating to say the site restoration will take around two weeks, but could take up to a month. OTW confirmed in an updated status report Friday morning that this outage is due to a security incident.

Some have speculated that the outage is a result of the PHP scramble this week that led to several sites going down to update their security, but AO3 doesn’t use PHP. An OTW representative told CNET : “I can let you know that this is not related to the PHP security issue as the Archive uses Ruby on Rails.”

Massive Fanfic Site Archive of Our Own Says It’s Going Down for 'Up to 4 Weeks'

A lot of people are grieving the loss of Kinktober, AO3’s annual group writing exercise where writers upload a chapter or fic every day throughout October based on a prompt of the day. (The prompts are horny, if that’s not clear.) Several of the writers and readers who reached out to me following the outage brought up the poor timing around Kinktober.

One writer I spoke to who posts her writing and reads others’ writing on AO3, told me that she was in the middle of racing to finish a work that was deliberately timed to Kinktober and Halloween when the outage happened. She was hitting “next chapter” while reading a fic on Wednesday night when she got the message that the site was down for maintenance, “which I initially took as a sign from the universe to go to bed,” she said.

“The outage hasn’t derailed my desire to write. If anything, I want to have more chapters ready to go so my readers can eat good once it’s over,” she said.

Do you know anything else about what happened to Ao3? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at sam.404. Otherwise, send me an email at sam@404media.co.

Some writers are considering posting elsewhere while they wait for AO3 to return, but it’s not an ideal workaround. AO3 author who goes by Selkie Myth told me they’re moving to Space Battles, another fanfiction site, during the outage. “I'm shrugging and just posting on SB [Space Battles] while the site's down. Hopefully I'll remember to post the chapters over on AO3 once it's back up — the story is projected to end during the outage. I anticipate the same is true for a lot of other authors,” they said.

Some people have said they’ll try fanfiction.net in the meantime, but it’s a much more bare-bones website. Fanfiction site Sufficient Velocity added a banner to its homepage welcoming AO3 refugees: “We’ve had a big influx of guests due to the AO3 outage. If you've been affected by the outage we're sorry to hear that and hope that they're able to get that fixed soon.” Wattpad, which many fanfiction writers and readers really, really hate for reasons I won’t get into here, posted on X: “we're here to support you during this difficult time.” Overwhelmingly, the replies are from people telling Wattpad to go away.

Another AO3 writer who goes by Ren told me she has two long works in progress right now with nowhere to post them. Posting elsewhere poses continuity and discovery problems, as some of these fanfiction works span chapters and hundreds of thousands of words of character and worldbuilding. “I could technically keep posting updates on sites like tumblr through the downtime, but both of these fics are quite long and I haven't been posting them anywhere other than AO3 — if I drop a new chapter for my 130k Pokemon Black and White fanfic on Tumblr completely out of context, people just now finding my work aren't going to be able to read the rest for a while :(“ she told me in an email. “I have seen other…

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-117549 📢 Source: openjs 💣 CVSS Score: 4.2 (MEDIUM) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False @fastify/secure-session is a session plugin for Fastify that stores an encrypted session in a cookie. In versions 7.5.0 through 8.4.1, when the plugin is configured with the signed cookie option, it calls the cookie unsign routine but, when the signature check reports the value as invalid, still passes the original cookie value to the session decoder, so a session whose signature did not validate is decrypted anyway. The practical effect appears when an application supplies the cookie signing secret independently of the session encryption key and rotates only the signing secret to retire existing sessions while keeping the encryption key active, because a holder of an old session cookie can strip the now obsolete signature and keep using the session. The attacker must already possess an unexpired encrypted session cookie and needs neither secret, and cannot forge session data, extend expiry, or survive rotation of the encryption key. The issue is fixed in @fastify/secure-session 8.4.2, which no longer decodes the session when the signed cookie option is set and the signature check fails, and users should upgrade to 8.4.2 or later. As a workaround, rotate the session encryption key rather than relying on rotation of the cookie signing secret alone. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-02T10:26:30.731Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-117549

items.content_ko: @fastify/secure-session은 암호화된 세션을 쿠키에 저장하는 Fastify 세션 플러그인이다. 7.5.0부터 8.4.1까지의 버전은 서명된 쿠키 옵션을 사용할 때 서명 검증이 실패해도 원래 쿠키 값을 세션 복호화기에 그대로 넘긴다. 그래서 서명이 검증되지 않은 세션도 복호화된다. 이 문제는 애플리케이션이 서명 비밀값을 세션 암호화 키와 별도로 관리하고, 기존 세션을 폐기하려고 서명 비밀값만 교체하며 암호화 키는 유지하는 경우에 드러난다. 이때 오래된 세션 쿠키를 가진 공격자는 이미 무효가 된 서명을 제거하고 세션을 계속 쓸 수 있다. 공격자는 만료되지 않은 암호화 세션 쿠키가 있어야 하지만 어떤 비밀값도 필요하지 않으며, 세션 데이터를 위조하거나 만료 시간을 연장하거나 암호화 키 교체 후에도 살아남을 수는 없다. 8.4.2에서는 서명된 쿠키 옵션이 켜져 있고 서명 검증이 실패하면 세션을 복호화하지 않도록 수정되었다.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: At A Worker-Run Game Studio, Employees Voted To Lose Their Jobs
items.content:
In early September, Montreal game studio KO-OP announced it would be “saying goodbye” to 13 people, citing–like so many others–difficulty finding funding. But unlike other layoffs in the games industry, which tend to strike suddenly from on-high, those affected had been involved in the decision from the beginning, and had actively voted for the outcome.

“As with all our company's operational decisions, this one was made democratically,” KO-OP wrote in its announcement. “Our members are regularly updated on our cash flow situation, and were made aware of this upcoming shortfall well in advance. Membership then appointed a group to plan for this eventuality, and ratified their recommendations. Team leads and our elected executives will also be impacted by these reductions. We believe this level of transparency and accountability ought to be a minimum requirement for all organizations.”

— KO_OP: 🪐 Wishlist Young Suns on Steam! ( @ko-op.com ) September 10, 2026 at 11:32 AM

It’s an unusual process for any company, but not necessarily one for KO-OP : The studio–which was founded in 2012, and has made games including Gnog, Goodbye Volcano High, and its current project Young Suns –operates as a co-operative. Everyone at the studio, which was roughly 30 people prior to the cuts, makes the same amount of money, $90K CAD ($63K USD). In addition to members’ game development work, they’re required to help with administrative tasks by joining committees dedicated to topics like hiring and finance, and membership meets every other month to talk as a group about how things are going and to vote on proposals about the studio.

“We try to call ourselves ‘worker run,’ because all of our operations are democratically operated and managed,” co-founder and studio director Saleem Dabbous told Aftermath over a video call, noting that the studio is still working toward legally becoming a co-op.

As the studio has grown, especially during production of Young Suns , its structure and operations have had to grow with it. Prior to the cuts, membership had elected a six-person “executive committee,” and it was this committee that was tasked with coming up with proposals for how to deal with KO-OP’s financial problems and, ultimately, who to let go.

Dabbous and former narrative designer Jenna Yow, who lost their job, largely referred to the cuts as furloughs, since KO-OP hopes to hire affected workers back. Affected workers are still eligible to receive any profits from Young Suns , and they can still attend studio meetings and vote on company decisions. They “still have the ability and the choice to be involved with the operations of the co-op at large, because it's in their best interest to see how things are progressing in case we're able to rehire them,” said Dabbous.

“With [a] layoff, generally, it's like a handshake, like a goodbye, it's done… Our intent is essentially to try to do the best we can by everybody, within our means, and to try to keep that as transparent as possible.”

And while workers didn’t know ahead of time who would be affected, they knew the cuts were coming and had time to prepare. This proved valuable for Yow, who was hired four and half years ago to work on narrative for Goodbye Volcano High as their first full-time job in the games industry out of college. During the furlough discussions, they had been trying to move to KO-OP’s Montreal office from the Seattle area. Aware they might not have a job and subsequently a visa if they moved, they were able to instead plan a move to live near family on the East Coast.

“Really the biggest benefit of it [was] just having the time to prepare… and then just kind of make plans accordingly, which is not something a lot of other people at other studios get to do,” Yow told Aftermath in the video call.

“Even though this situation is not one I would wish on anybody, I do feel like it's probably the best way it could have happened for anyone.”

items.title: Introducing Kwi, a new KDE terminal emulator
items.summary: linux
items.content:
Introducing Kwi, a new KDE terminal emulator

I've started work on a new KDE application. It's called Kwi (pronounced kwee ).

Kwi is designed to provide users of KDE Plasma and other free desktops with a modern and fast terminal, built on a robust tech stack and following the latest KDE HIG and UI conventions.

In some sense, the product vision for Kwi is to be kind of unexciting: Just what you want and expect out of a KDE Plasma terminal. Of course, given the powerful nature users generally expect from KDE software, this does not make the project lacking in ambition. :-)

To achieve things, Kwi builds on libghostty-vt from the excellent Ghostty project and familiar, mature KDE Frameworks such as KPty . It has a very speedy GPU-accelerated (Vulkan or OpenGL) renderer powered by the Qt Scene Graph. Its user interface is built with the latest and greatest by Kirigami , making it blend in very well among more recent KDE applications and the Plasma desktop.

In keeping with the theme, Kwi's icon/logo is a cute little terminal ghost. This is also how it came to bear its name: kwisin , or more typically gwisin , is a romanized form of 귀신 - Korean for ghost. It's pronounced a little bit like kwee-shin .

Compared to the venerable and mature Konsole , Kwi is young and new. At the moment it offers a more streamlined feature set than Konsole, carefully realized using KDE's latest HIG patterns. The way forward will be to build on this slowly and carefully, using everything we've learned as a community about running mature design processes over the last decade or so (hello, VDG!). It's a chance to canvass the scene, take stock of how other terminals implement more recent innovations in this space, and compete with a KDE spin on things.

Konsole is very intertwined with the older of the two user interface tech stacks in Qt, QWidget . QWidget typically renders using the CPU, and so does Konsole. Newer KDE software (including Plasma itself) typically uses Qt Quick and benefits from GPU acceleration via Vulkan or OpenGL instead. This is what Kwi does as well. For certain terminal applications the performance gain (3x-35x faster than Konsole depending on what's being benchmarked) can make an actual big difference in the user experience, but generally it should also help reduce battery usage.

Kwi is built on libghostty-vt , a project that describes itself as an ecosystem play - provide a headless lib that takes care of all the gnarly terminal parsing and state, enable downstream projects and become sort of a rising tide that lifts all boats. It's starting to really deliver on this promise lately, outpacing other terminal implementations on support for modern TUI features and not hoarding all this good only for itself. While the library will only make an ABI/API stable v1.0 promise at some point in the next 4-6 months, it's already slowly being adopted by big and popular projects, including Neovim, Ghostel and many more. Here's a list .

Kwi marries the library to the KDE/Qt tech stack, which allows the project to focus mostly on desktop integration and rendering performance, two areas where KDE's software stack is generally second to none. The combination of the two offers some improvements over Konsole already, for example:

General UI lift-up to the latest KDE HIG

3x–35x faster overall performance, depending on the benchmark E.g. 870 fps in DOOM-fire-zig on a test system, vs. 23 fps in Konsole

Rendering GPU-accelerated rendering via Vulkan or OpenGL

Better support for using the KDE Plasma system color scheme, including live changes

Improved support for correct handling of Wayland fractional scaling

Improved terminal text rendering Improved rendering of text decorations (e.g. z-sorting for complex underline styles)

Improved support for ligatures, especially when they interact with coloration and selection

Support for mode-2027 grapheme widths, Nerd Font icon scaling, etc.

Improved support for Powerline and geometry symbols

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Lenovo's 'encrypted' fingerprint USB drive is just an unencrypted SD card in a fancy case
items.content:
Security researcher Xusheng Li found that a Lenovo ThinkPlus FU100 fingerprint USB stick, sold as an AES-256-encrypted device for data security, ended up being just a plain SD card internally, HackingPassion reports. The fingerprint reader only enabled the USB connection, and nothing on the card was actually encrypted. An AI-assisted follow-up last week discovered what Li calls backdoor accounts on another maker’s drive, as well as hardcoded keys in other supposedly secure USB storage products.

Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers

America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price

GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year

Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible

The FU100 is “just an SD card in a fancy case,” Li said in a March conference talk. It is, as a result, trivial for anyone with physical access to get to the drive’s data. One of his takeaways: “‘Hardware security’ can be pure marketing.” This isn’t the first time drive makers’ own encryption has failed , and it won’t be the last.

The original ThinkPlus FU100 analysis happened last year, with an interim fix using epoxy over the card. A later fix by Lenovo, put out early this year for the FU100, FU200 and TU800 drives, as well as the TSD303 SSD, requires owners to call a China service line, then either send devices back for replacement or get an on-site firmware upgrade. Lenovo advises backing up data first and strongly recommends wiping the drive before sending it in, which is quite an inconvenience. Lenovo rated the advisory’s severity as high, and one of its three CVEs covers the configuration software, which could let a local, logged-in user bypass device authentication and enroll an untrusted fingerprint.

The same research also turned up a different flaw in Lenovo’s TSD303 external SSD. Its data actually was encrypted, but the drive sent the correct password back over USB in plain text for the software to compare, making it easy to capture. The first fix came three months after the initial report, using block cipher encryption with a key derived from a timestamp-like value. Lenovo’s software could derive that key, and the first software fix is vulnerable if taken apart, making it not useful for protecting data if a device is stolen. A later fix, late last year, has the drive check the typed password itself, so the correct one never leaves the drive.

The same software development kit used for the drive covered nine other devices from multiple vendors, most of which could also reveal passwords to a savvy actor. In addition, two left data unencrypted on a microSD card. The full list of vendors was blacked out on Li’s slides.

AI agent use for driving reverse-engineering tools continues to increase. AI has also been exposing more security flaws recently. Li used OpenAI’s Codex, an AI programming-centric tool, with his employer’s reverse-engineering tool against other vendors’ protection schemes. Netac’s tool took about seven minutes to break, as Codex found a fixed key built into the program, along with the user’s password written to diagnostic logs.

Copy protection differs from direct access, as the intent is to allow the recipient to view files, just not make copies of them. KakaSoft’s USB Copy Protection has an internal password the program builds itself, which Codex rebuilt to decrypt a test file without the user’s password in around 26 minutes. Nexcopy’s Copy Secure took about 10 minutes, with its key unlocked by a certificate built into the viewer app. Separately, SecZure’s YutianDun has two hidden “backdoor” accounts with simple passwords, discovered with time-travel debugging, stepping through a timeline trace. However, Li’s comments suggest that malicious intent cannot be assumed.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-120215 📢 Source: openjs 💣 CVSS Score: 3.7 (LOW) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False @fastify/cors is the CORS plugin for the Fastify web framework. In versions 8.2.0 through 11.3.x, an application that registers the plugin with the non-default onSend hook option crashes on a CORS preflight. On an OPTIONS request that carries the Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method headers, the plugin calls reply.send from inside the onSend hook and re-enters the send pipeline, so a second write of the response headers throws an uncaught ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT that can terminate the Node.js process when no process-level handler is installed. An unauthenticated remote client can trigger this with a single preflight request, so the impact is availability only, and exploitation requires the non-default onSend configuration. The issue is fixed in @fastify/cors 11.4.0, where onSend is no longer an accepted hook value and registration fails with a clear error instead of crashing at request time, and users should upgrade to 11.4.0 or later. As a workaround, use any other hook such as the default onRequest, or set preflight to false. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-02T10:20:47.667Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-120215
