items.title: The AI cost of JavaScript frameworks
items.content:
One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will “supercharge” your development, the right abstraction will benefit both you and your users ( DX and UX all in one!). All of this breathless boasting is usually offered with zero evidence. Alex Russell has called this “frontend’s lost decade” , Baldur Bjarnason has called programming a pop culture , and I’ve tried to counter this trend in my blog with facts and benchmarks (at my best, anyway).

For a long time it seemed like our community’s allergy to evidence was driven by the desire for greater DX . In other words, devs just liked the way it felt to type JSX in React, and the arguments promoting React or related tools (“the virtual DOM is fast!”) were largely post-hoc rationalizations to justify those initial gut feelings. ( Jonathan Haidt would likely agree with this assessment.)

But in the agentic era, when developers are no longer typing code by hand and are thus less constrained by DX, I still see vibes ruling the day (and not just in the sense of “vibe-coding”). Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc. Once again, these claims are often made without evidence. Whenever I read one of these accounts, I think to myself, “Where are the benchmarks?”

Well I got curious, so I wrote a benchmark. The structure of this benchmark is pretty straightforward:

Design a small but non-trivial Pokémon app using the PokéAPI (those who have followed my work will be unsurprised)

Instruct agents to build the app with a particular JavaScript framework/meta-framework (e.g. Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, etc.)

Test the output against a spec conformance suite (to avoid agent cheating)

Evaluate the results in terms of development time, tokens spent, lines of code, and performance and accessibility scores in Lighthouse

The app is fairly simple: you’ve got a list of Pokémon with their types, moves, and data from various games. You can search, filter, etc.:

I should start off with some caveats: this is not a perfect experiment. This app represents only one holotype – it’s a relatively content-based site with little interactivity, closer to a Wikipedia than a Figma, GMail, etc. That said, I had to choose some app to build, and this one is at least easy to understand at a high level, and relatively straightforward to spec out and test.

To try to even the playing field, I had each framework/meta-framework use the official MCP or skills for that tool. I wanted to avoid accusations of “this framework is not well-represented in the training data, that’s why we built our MCP, we expect people to use it,” etc. I also didn’t over-specify the exact architecture to use (e.g. SSR vs CSR ), nor did I specify that the app should be as performant as possible. I simply gave the spec to Opus 5.5 with high effort and told it to use the latest version of the given framework. Each agent ran in a sandbox and without any knowledge that it would be tested in Lighthouse on performance and accessibility, although it was given the conformance test suite.

Note I also didn’t mandate any CSS methodology, except to avoid using Tailwind, Bootstrap, or any other component framework, and to design based on a set of spec tokens to enforce some visual consistency. I didn’t want to make this test all about CSS, but instead about JS frameworks, CSR vs SSR, SPAs vs MPAs , etc. The resulting app is tested against a conformance suite based on the accessibility tree rather than the raw DOM to avoid mandating any particular HTML structure – one framework uses web components which rely on shadow DOM, so this was required.

items.title: JPEG XS - Wikipedia
items.summary: graphics
items.content:
JPEG XS ( standardized as ISO/IEC 21122) is an image and video codec that offers both visually and mathematically lossless quality. It is a special-purpose codec that is specifically designed to allow for low-complexity and low-latency implementations. [ 2 ] [ 3 ] Target applications of the standard include streaming high-quality content for professional video over IP (SMPTE ST 2022 and ST 2110 ) in broadcast and other applications: virtual reality , drones, autonomous vehicles using cameras, gaming. [ 2 ] [ 4 ] [ 5 ] Although there is not an official acronym definition, XS was chosen to highlight the extra small and extra speed characteristics of the codec.

Relying on these key features, JPEG XS is suitable for any application where uncompressed content is the norm, yet still allowing for significant savings in the required bandwidth usage, preserving quality and low latency. Among the targeted use cases are video transport over professional video links (like SDI and professional video over IP ), real-time video storage, memory buffers, omnidirectional video capture and rendering, and image sensor compression (for example in cameras and in the automotive industry). [ 6 ] JPEG XS favors visually lossless quality in combination with low latency and low complexity, over data reduction through compression. It is not a direct competitor to alternative image codecs like JPEG 2000 and JPEG XL or video codecs like AV1 , AVC/H.264 and HEVC/H.265 which tend to focus on compression efficiency.

JPEG XS is actively used in several application domains. [ 10 ]

Video bandwidth requirements are growing as video resolutions, frame rates, bit depths, and the number of video streams are constantly increasing. Although the capacities of video links and communication channels are also growing, there are applications where the reduced data rate afforded by JPEG-XS is advantageous.

Both the broadcast and pro-AV markets are shifting towards AV-over-IP-based infrastructure, with a preference going to Gigabit Ethernet links for remote production and faster fiber-based Ethernet for in-house facilities. Given the available bandwidth and infrastructure cost, relying on uncompressed video may be cost-prohibitive if 4K, 8K, increased bit depths for HDR, and higher frame rates need to be supported.

With XS, it is, for example, possible to repurpose existing SDI cables to transport 4K60 over a single 3G-SDI (at 4:1 compression ratio), and even over a single HD-SDI (at 8:1 compression ratio). Similar scenarios can be used to transport 8K60 content over various SDI cable types (e.g., 6G-SDI and 12G-SDI). Alternatively, XS enables transporting 4K60 content over Gigabit Ethernet and 8K60 over 5G or 10 Gigabit Ethernet , which would be impossible without compression.

The following table shows expected compression ranges for some typical use cases.

Related to the transport of video streams is the storage and retrieval of high-resolution streams where bandwidth limitations similarly apply. For instance, video cameras use internal storage like SSD drives or SD cards to record high-resolution streams of images, yet the maximum data rates of such storage devices may be below that required to store uncompressed video in real time.

JPEG XS has built-in support for the direct compression of RAW Bayer /CFA images using the Star-Tetrix Color Transform. This transform takes a RAW Bayer pattern image and decorrelates the samples into a 4-component image with each component having only a quarter of the resolution. [ 11 ] This means that the total amount of samples to further process and compress remains the same, yet the values are decorrelated similarly to a classical Multiple Component Transform.

Avoiding such conversion prevents information loss and allows this processing step to be done outside of the camera. This is advantageous because it allows deferring demosaicing the Bayer content from the moment of capturing to the production phase, where choices regarding…

items.title: Innocent People Are Being Accused of Shoplifting by Faulty AI-Facial Recognition Systems at an Alarming Rate: "It's the stuff of Kafkaesque nightmares."
items.content:
From New York City to the streets of Tokyo , creepy AI-facial recognition security systems are quickly becoming a common sight across the world. Unfortunately for many, the tech is nowhere near ready for the responsibility of live use as the troubling rise of false-positive matches makes clear.

In the United Kingdom, AI surveillance systems in retail stores have led to a surge in customers being wrongly accused of shoplifting. TechRadar highlighted a number of recent cases throughout the country, where shoppers say false accusations have left them shaken, with a feeling that their privacy had been horribly violated.

As one woman identified as Mary told the publication, her husband has been socially “isolated” after a quick jaunt into a Home Bargains store for vitamins went awry. When the stores’ system flagged the anonymous man as a shoplifter, the couple was forced to leave by management, seemingly without any chance to refute the accusation.

“I was scared to go into a shop,” the man told TechRadar .

Another man was said to be “shaking from head to toe” following his wife’s removal from a Budgens chain store for the crime of stealing “loads of meat” days before — an accusation complicated by the fact that they hadn’t set foot in the store for months.

In these and other cases, the publication reports a dizzying labyrinth of corporate bureaucracy and vague insinuations that leave innocent people unable to access their local businesses, and with little recourse to clear their name.

In the UK, individuals can file Subject Access Requests, or SARs, which are like US-Freedom of Information Act requests but for private companies. Though the avenue technically exists for those wrongly accused of shoplifting, it’s a massive undertaking just for the hope of clearing your name — and requires handing over even more private information to private companies.

As head of advocacy at civil liberty group Big Brother Watch Jack Coulson told TechRadar , it’s “the stuff of Kafkaesque nightmares to be trapped in a maze of bureaucracy and forced to hand over even more personal data just to be told the accusation.”

items.title: Mathematics has changed. Let's act like it
items.content:
Updates on my research and expository papers, discussion of open problems, and other maths-related topics. By Terence Tao

1 November, 2026 in guest blog , opinion | Tags: Frank Calegari | by Terence Tao

[This is a guest post by Frank Calegari . This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

The release by OpenAI on October 6 of over 700 research papers was a watershed in the history of mathematics. AI is now undeniably capable of making groundbreaking contributions across many areas of mathematics. So why are some mathematicians so unhappy?

Some of it is the apparent disregard by AI companies for the practice of mathematics. The OpenAI papers — despite some tremendous ideas — are atrociously written and violate our community expectations of attribution. Some of them are even wrong. We have much more control over how we hire mathematicians, publish papers, and train students than over the behavior of trillion-dollar companies, and that is where our efforts would be better spent.

Much of the reaction seems to reflect a feeling that the subject that they love is under attack, and is being “hollowed out”. The recent OpenAI dump made barely a dent on the general problems of functoriality and reciprocity in the Langlands program. But even if it had solved every problem in the Langlands program, to imagine that would have “solved number theory” would be as naive as saying that the construction of the periodic table solved chemistry. Mathematicians should do a better job explaining that when we talk about the central problems in any area, we are merely discussing the most natural boundaries of our understanding — and that unlocking them is not the end but the first step to finding new playgrounds to explore. Of course, this takes time. I looked for areas of mathematics which were “harder hit”. It is hard not to be struck by Hugo Duminil-Copin’s lament :

Not a single one of the major open problems I have publicly mentioned throughout my career (whether in a talk, a lecture, an article, or even a grant proposal) was left untouched by the announcement. Everything has been claimed to be proved.

I expected to see a few of them in the list. But not all of them. Not all at once. Not with such nonchalance.

The classification of finite simple groups.

I can’t say much about percolation theory, but there is another historical precedent I think mathematicians should take note of. In 1972, Dan Gorenstein announced a program towards the classification of finite simple groups. After a flurry of activity over around a decade, the “classification” was announced by Gorenstein in 1983 (somewhat prematurely, with the case of quasithin groups not being completed for another two decades by Aschbacher and Smith).

The classification of finite simple groups was in many ways a huge success, but it was also a failure in that it — apologies to my group theorist friends and collaborators — cooled a lot of the interest around the subject. The “famous problem” had gone, and mathematicians on the whole turned their attention elsewhere. And yet, there remain very rich questions in finite group theory and even about the classification itself (to name just one: John Conway’s favorite question is why does the Monster group exist? ). Perhaps for some fields, the OpenAI dump feels like how a group theorist may have felt in 1970 if the classification was dumped in their office, not in the form of the actual papers, but printed out on a spirit duplicator, smudged a little, then spread randomly like confetti all over the floor.

Right now, we need efforts like that of Gorenstein, Lyons, and Solomon and their work on the revised classification. If this was all we had to do, then it would be a fairly thankless task. But we also have the responsibility not to pronounce the subject “done” but rather — with these new tools available — ripe for further investigation. items.title_ko: 수학은 달라졌다, 이제 그에 맞게 행동하자
items.summary_ko: Terence Tao 블로그의 게스트 글로, Frank Calegari가 작성했다. 2026년 10월 6일 OpenAI가 700편이 넘는 연구 논문을 공개한 것을 계기로 AI가 수학의 여러 분야에서 획기적인 기여를 할 수 있음이 분명해졌다고 짚는다. 일부 수학자들이 불안해하는 이유는 AI 기업들이 수학 연구의 관행을 무시하고 있다는 점과, 자신들이 사랑하는 분야가 '속이 비어가고' 있다는 느낌 때문이라고 설명한다.
items.content_ko: Terence Tao의 블로그 'Mathematics has changed. Let's act like it'에 실린 Frank Calegari의 게스트 글이다. 원문은 이 글이 다른 파일 형식으로 작성된 뒤 AI로 변환되었다고 밝히고 있다. 글은 2026년 10월 6일 OpenAI가 700편 이상의 연구 논문을 공개한 것이 수학사에서 분수령이 되었다고 평가한다. AI가 여러 수학 분야에서 획기적인 기여를 할 수 있다는 점은 이제 부정할 수 없다는 것이다. 그럼에도 일부 수학자들이 불만스러워하는 이유로, 글은 AI 기업들이 수학의 실천 방식을 무시하고 있다는 점을 든다. OpenAI의 논문들은 훌륭한 아이디어를 담고 있지만 글쓰기가 매우 형편없고, 학계의 저자 표기(attribution) 관행을 위반하며, 일부는 틀리기까지 했다고 지적한다. 글쓴이는 수학자들이 조직하고 통제할 수 있는 영역은 채용, 논문 게재, 학생 교육이라며, 조 단위 규모의 기업들의 행동을 바꾸려 하기보다 그쪽에 노력을 기울이는 편이 낫다고 주장한다. 많은 반응의 밑바탕에는 자신이 사랑하는 학문이 공격받고 '속이 비어가고' 있다는 감정이 있다고 보고 있다. 원문은 여기서 잘려 있다.

This site is supported by donations to The OEIS Foundation .

We are pleased to announce the winning sequences in the OEIS 400k celebration. Well over 100 nominations were received, covering a great many topics collectively showing that the spirit of the OEIS is alive and well.

The selection committee consisted of Sean A. Irvine , Jonas Karlsson , Hugo Pfoertner , and Neil J. A. Sloane . Committee members abstained from providing evaluations on sequences they authored or were closely involved with. The selection committee would like to thank all the people who took time to nominate a sequence.

The city-building sequence: a(n) = the height h of the shortest building which can see exactly h earlier buildings.

The height of a building in Eric Fox's City-Building sequence is determined by how many existing buildings it can see. This impressed all the judges as by far the most brilliant invention of 2026. There are already 25 other sequences that reference it.

A399995 (previously A394611 ) Joshua B. Weinstein

a(1) = 0. For n > 1, a(n) is the number of ways to write a(n-1) as the sum of two earlier terms with distinct positions in the sequence. A simple definition leading to a frustratingly difficult unsolved problem.

A399996 (previously A400866 ) Dmitry Kamenetsky

Number of free polyominoes with 2n cells that can be dissected into two congruent polyominoes. The best polyomino sequence of the year.

a(n) is the maximum number of distinct positive differences of an n-element subset of {0, 1, ..., n*(n-1)/2}. An instant classic extremal set-theory problem.

A399998 (previously A400887 ) Rok Cestnik

a(n+1) = a(n-a(a(n))^2) + 1, a(0) = 0. A new twist on the classic Hofstadter recurrences.

A399999 (previously A400462 ) Ed Pegg Jr

Number of ways to cut a 30-60-90 triangle into n 30-60-90 triangles. One of several triangle dissection problems, lovely pictures.

A400001 (previously A400663 ) Felix Huber

a(n) is the number of congruence classes of nondegenerate triangles whose vertices are points of an n X n X n grid. One of several excellent Huber sequences relating to triangles.

A400002 (previously A400976 ) Aidan Markey

Start with a set of two adjacent points in a hexagonal lattice. At each iteration, add to the set the lattice points which are adjacent to exactly two points already in the set, but only if those two points are adjacent to each other. The sequence gives the number of points in the set after n iterations. An unusual sequence of clusters.

A400003 (previously A399179 ) Michael S. Branicky and N. J. A. Sloane

The sequence of binary decisions that defines the unique infinite path in the base-10 comma child graph. Previously MSB/NJAS had to use Koenig's Lemma and the Axiom of Choice to show that it was possible for the kangaroo to escape death. Chris Randall and Paul Roberts showed without using AI that there is a unique path with a simple recurrence.

A400004 (previously A401021 ) Scott B. Farrar

Half the minimum surface area of a rectangular box with positive integer side lengths and volume at least n. A new problem with a classic feel.

A400005 (previously A395645 ) Rémy Sigrist

Consider the square spiral with its cells numbered starting at 0. Three players, Red, Green and Blue, take turns and place knights at the smallest unoccupied cell not attacked by an existing knight of a different color. Sequence lists squares occupied by a Red knight. A representative of many astonishing sequences of knights on an infinite chessboard, a popular topic after a Numberphile video appeared.

These are a further ten nominated sequences which the committee found particularly attractive or interesting. These sequences have all received the keyword “nice” but retain their original A-numbers.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

The upsell was reported in The Atlantic , which found that SpaceX, which operates Starlink, advised that Ukraine switch to a more expensive plan to avoid service interruptions when asked about the outage.

“If anything can yet restrain Musk from abandoning Ukraine, it may be his own financial interests,” The Atlantic reported this week. “Earlier this month, when U.S. military officials asked SpaceX about the outages in Ukraine, the company advised switching to an upgraded contract to restore Ukraine’s access, U.S. officials told us.”

The incident came just four months after SpaceX’s IPO this June. Reports have suggested that Starlink has already made hundreds of millions of dollars providing Ukraine and its military with internet service since the start of Russia’s invasion.

Early in the war, Musk supposedly “donated” thousands of Starlink satellite kits to the country, making much of Ukraine dependent on the service that holds a relative monopoly over satellite network systems and Ukraine’s ability to conduct critical military operations, such as drone piloting.

The New York Times reported in 2023 that the company is charging $2,500 per terminal per month, with over 42,000 Starlink terminals in use across the country. The co-founder of the Ukraine Defense Fund, which has helped secure Starlink access for the Ukrainian military, told The Atlantic that he estimates there are now over 250,000 Starlink terminals in use across the war zone.

Musk’s capping of service was met with outrage earlier this month , sparking panic within both the Ukrainian and U.S. governments as a large swath of the country’s military was effectively out of service. “Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. May you burn in hell.”

Musk’s seeming turn on Ukraine comes as the Trump administration is increasingly embracing Russia and cutting funding to Ukraine.

The incident has shined a spotlight on Musk’s vast ability to control world events and swing the favor of an entire war toward one side if he so chooses — an enormous amount of power left to one man who represents nothing but his own whims and profits.

Despite this, the Pentagon’s inspector general is effectively refusing to investigate Musk’s interruptions to the service, it told Congress this week.

Critics have already raised concerns about the enormous control that Starlink has over space in low orbit, while its services are the only option in many places that otherwise lack connectivity. items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-120214 📢 Source: openjs 💣 CVSS Score: 5.9 (MEDIUM) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False @fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP requests to an upstream server under a configured prefix. In versions 11.6.0 through 11.6.2, the destination validation normalizes literal backslashes before it percent-decodes the request path, so a path that encodes its backslashes and dot-segments survives the dot-segment check and is only turned into backslash and double-dot sequences after that check has passed. When the upstream resolves on a platform that treats a backslash as a path separator, the forwarded request walks out of the configured proxy prefix and reaches a sibling location on the upstream. An unauthenticated remote attacker can use this to retrieve upstream resources outside the intended prefix, so the impact is confidentiality only, and exploitation depends on the upstream's path handling. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.3, and users should upgrade to 11.6.3 or later. This is a follow-up to the earlier prefix-escape fix, which did not account for the encoded-backslash form. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-02T10:07:08.695Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-120214
items.title_ko: [CVE-2026-120214] @fastify/http-proxy 인코딩된 백슬래시로 프록시 경로 이탈 가능 (CVSS 5.9, MEDIUM)
items.summary_ko: @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.0~11.6.2에서 경로 검증 순서 문제로, 인증되지 않은 원격 공격자가 프록시 prefix 바깥의 업스트림 리소스를 조회할 수 있다. 백슬래시를 경로 구분자로 처리하는 플랫폼에서 발생하며 기밀성에만 영향을 준다. CVSS 점수는 5.9(MEDIUM)이다. 11.6.3에서 수정되었으므로 해당 버전 이상으로 업그레이드하라고 권고한다. 이전 prefix 이탈 수정이 인코딩된 백슬래시 형태를 고려하지 않았던 데서 이어지는 후속 취약점이다.
items.content_ko: @fastify/http-proxy는 설정된 prefix 아래의 HTTP 요청을 업스트림 서버로 전달하는 Fastify 플러그인이다. 11.6.0부터 11.6.2까지 버전에서는 목적지 검증이 요청 경로를 퍼센트 디코딩하기 전에 리터럴 백슬래시를 정규화한다. 따라서 백슬래시와 dot-segment를 인코딩한 경로는 dot-segment 검사를 통과하고, 검사 이후에야 백슬래시와 이중 점(..) 시퀀스로 바뀐다. 업스트림이 백슬래시를 경로 구분자로 처리하는 플랫폼에서 실행되면, 전달된 요청이 설정된 프록시 prefix를 벗어나 업스트림의 형제 위치에 도달한다. 인증되지 않은 원격 공격자는 이를 이용해 의도한 prefix 바깥의 업스트림 리소스를 가져올 수 있다. 영향은 기밀성에 한정되며, 악용 여부는 업스트림의 경로 처리 방식에 따라 달라진다. 11.6.3에서 수정되었으며, 해당 버전 이상으로 업그레이드하라고 권고한다. 이는 앞서 나온 prefix 이탈 수정이 인코딩된 백슬래시 형태를 고려하지 않았던 데서 이어지는 후속 이슈다.

items.title: Instagram Meta AI Vulnerability: How Hackers Bypassed 2FA with Prompt Injection
items.content:
Update 5: Instagram is now leaking recovery email and phone numbers linked to an account.

Seems like every day a new security issue crops up at Instagram.

Instagram Exposing Linked Email and Phone Number

Update 4: A new report suggests that Instagram accounts may be vulnerable to coordinated mass-report abuse. According to the claim, when a newly created account is routed through a Los Angeles-based VPN and then submits a specific mix of reports in scam and fraud category, the targeted account can allegedly be banned without any human review.

Instagram Account Banning by AI by Reporting Scam and Fraud (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 3: Meta’s apparent fix for the AI bot vulnerability is difficult to take seriously. Instead of fully disabling the risky functionality, they reportedly removed it from the visible interface while leaving the underlying API endpoint accessible. Hiding the button may stop regular users from seeing the feature, but it does nothing if attackers can still reach the same workflow directly through the API.

Meta Hid AI Chatbot from UI (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 2: Yet another Instagram account-takeover trick is reportedly being abused, this time involving Meta’s AI chatbot. Sellers are allegedly using modified Instagram builds on Android emulators like BlueStacks, then manipulating the AI with hidden characters and carefully worded prompts to force username changes. The method is reportedly being used to grab rare OG handles, including one-letter usernames, and handle-monitoring bots have already flagged several suspicious swaps.

New Instagram AI Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 1: A new exploit, which is even worse than this one is currently doing rounds on telegram. Details unknown at this time. Unpatched at the time of writing.

New Instagram Unpatched Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

Allegedly, the new method is via Facebook recovery. Apparently, prompting Meta AI to turn on “Development Mode” and attaching proof of account compromise along with email works. More details awaited.

There’s a version of this story where it reads like a hypothetical from a conference talk. An AI agent with elevated backend privileges. A natural language interface sitting in front of account-level APIs. No hard authentication gate before executing state changes. Someone in the audience raises their hand and says, “that’s a disaster waiting to happen.” Everyone nods.

That hypothetical played out in production over the weekend.

A logical flaw in Meta’s AI-powered Instagram account recovery assistant let attackers bypass two-factor authentication entirely not by cracking a code or intercepting an SMS, but by talking the chatbot into doing the work for them. High-value “OG” Instagram handles worth hundreds of thousands of dollars were stolen and resold on Telegram within minutes of each compromise. The dormant Obama White House account got hijacked. Prominent researchers woke up locked out of their own profiles.

Meta’s solution was to deploy a conversational AI layer to handle common recovery workflows: relinking a lost email address, triggering a password reset, verifying account ownership. items.title: AI agent swarms unleashed in Minecraft to ‘build a thriving civilization’ — 50-agent teams fail after falling into paralyzing bureaucracy: It is hoped game testing can provide insight into recent AI.
items.content:
AI researchers at ycombinator and Olam Labs recently tested AI agent swarms in gaming scenarios. Minecraft and its various game modes were the sandboxes where 100s of agents were unleashed to work together or as adversaries. The idea seems to be that the in-game collaborations and conflicts would provide insight into real-world headline-grabbing cases with AI agents involved.

This study might help us see what happened, good and bad, in recent AI swarm cases, and thus developers of this technology can improve it. The blog mentions two contrasting cases, which were the thousand-agent swarms that “recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems,” and the “extremely dangerous” OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. This research is built on prior work and frameworks, specifically repos like Mindcraft and scripting tools in Mineflayer.

The first AI swarm testing plan was a simple collaborative one. During this test phase, the researchers tasked 50 agents with building a thriving civilization in three hours. It seems to have tested 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents here, but not any Claude agents .

Probably the most interesting insight from this ‘Civ50’ test was that the 50-strong colony never really thrived. After the first night saw zombies take out a large number of agents (but with little penalty) it was noted that “many ambitious initial tasks were abandoned.”

From then on, the colonists cautiously survived, and there was a tendency toward bureaucracy. As an example, “four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a ‘sole fertilizer operator’ for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block.” The researchers say this AI agent swarm behavior “felt similar to patterns seen while working with coding agents.”

(Image credit: ycombinator ) Next up, the researchers decided to put AI agent swarms into conflict. First they tested them in Bed Wars, which is a kind of team PvP capture the base, while defending yours game mode. The setup was 10 GPT‑6.1 Sol vs. 10 Claude Opus 5.5 agents.

“GPT agents came up with much more aggressive and elaborate strategies,” noted the researchers. Claude was more defensive. It was also interesting to observe contrasts in how the teams handled problems. “A tool bug stopped block-breaking. GPT diagnosed it and shared workarounds; several Claudes concluded breaking was impossible.”

Finally, the agents were tested in Mindustry, a kind of light RTS combat game with tower defense mode in Minecraft. “The GPTs won 6-1 against the Claudes in the 7 games,” which was a great result for the OpenAI-created agents. Researchers concluded that GPTs acted more like a hive, while Claudes had a single leader but a democratic-style decision process. In Mindustry, the former was the foundation for a more consistently winning strategy.

These swarms are open sourced so you can run your own, if you are interested in tweaking and testing. The source blog post ends with some open questions that you can check hands-on, offering some directions for investigative probing. For example, it is suggested that comparing different mixes of models and varying sizes of agent swarms in Minecraft might raise worthwhile conclusions.

items.title: The case against Makefiles
items.content:
You don’t need a Makefile. Whatever your use-case, there is a better tool.

Makefiles are archaic technology, living on by force of inertia and notalgia. The syntax is opaque and the error messages are unhelpful. It’s time to move on.

As far as I can see, there are two remaining use cases for Makefiles in the wild:

running arbitrary tasks that have dependencies between each other.

Makefiles are no longer the best solution for either of these use cases,

Makefiles are the original build system. The make program was born in 1976 at Bell Labs, out of a frustration with existing build scripts (piles of sh ). The concepts it pionneered ( e.g. the build graph) are still the basis of modern build systems, but the ergonomics of build systems have improved a lot since then.

Aside: Build scripts, makefiles, and other build systems

Let’s step back into 1976, and write a build script for our program like they would have in the pioneer days.

# Compile the individual source files to object files

# Link the object files into an executable

Forget to add a cc command to build a source file? Now you’re linking with an old version of the file that you compiled by hand.

Using modern bash features, we could improve the script quite a bit.

Using a bash variable expansion to replace .c with .o allows us to use re-use the list of sources in both the compile commands and the linker command. For a small example program, this approach works, but it doesn’t scale well: we rebuild all the sources each time we run, regardless of whether they need to be rebuilt or not.

The similarities are quite obvious. The most significant difference between the script and the makfile is what they describe. The script is an imperative procedure: it lays out the steps that need to be accomplished to build the final binary, and executes them all in sequence, every time. The makefile describes the dependencies between inputs and outputs. This allows the makefile to skip steps that are redundant because the input has not changed.

The cost of this change is syntax. The build script is relatively easy to read but the makefile is full of magic tokens. What are $@ , and $< ? To an experienced practitioner, they are obvious. For me, they require a trip to google each time (or if I actually remember, a trip into The Sum of All Knowledge , my knowledgebase in Obsidian ).

Compare this with an equivalent CMake script

executable ( 'myexe' , [ 'main.c' , 'lib.c' ])

Without knowing anything about CMake or meson, the goal of the scripts is quite clear. The knowledge of how to actually build an executable or a library is hidden which is a shame, but the intent is clear.

The fundamental mistake of Make is that it describes the edges of the build graph, not the nodes. It describes the operations required to transform one file into another, but never describes the goal of the transformation.

To build a file, we say that there exists a node %.c and a node %.o , and that to go from %.c to %.o , it is necessary to apply $( CC ) $( CFLAGS ) -c -o $@ $< to %.c . A no point does this say anything about what we are trying to achieve.

In CMake, to build an executable, we use add_executable(app main.c lib.c) . This describes the end goal, not the transformation. This is not to say that CMake is the perfect build-system, far from that, but it is at least easier to follow.

Build-systems that describe intent, and not transformations, have one property that most Makefiles in the wild lack: they work reliably when run in parallel. Most makefiles I have had the misfortune of encountering fail when run in parallel. To build reliably, build scripts become

make -j $( nproc ) all || make -j $( nproc ) all || make -j $( nproc ) all

This is definitely a skill issue . But a tool too complicated for the average C programmer inside a boring company is no longer a good tool.

Make aficionados love to tell new victims how great their makefiles are: they are invariably better than whatever sub-par…

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-120213 📢 Source: openjs 💣 CVSS Score: 9.1 (CRITICAL) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False @fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP requests to an upstream server under a configured prefix. In versions 9.0.0 through 11.6.5, when an application uses parameterized prefix and rewritePrefix options to pin clients to a fixed upstream path, the plugin substitutes URL-decoded route parameters into rewritePrefix without re-encoding them. A parameter value that encodes a path separator together with a fragment or query delimiter therefore decodes into real separators and delimiters that inject extra upstream path segments and strip the mandatory suffix the rewritePrefix was meant to enforce, without using any dot-dot traversal. An unauthenticated remote attacker can use this to reach upstream locations outside the intended prefix, leading to path-restriction bypass and, depending on the upstream, server-side request forgery or authorization bypass in the proxied service. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.6, and users should upgrade to 11.6.6 or later. items.summary: databases, testing
items.content:
Modern applications often spread state across a variety of systems:

databases, caches, queues, data warehouses, search indices, and so on.

Coordinating these systems is challenging: caches are often stale, the

analytics platform might lag days behind the primary database, the

search index might lose data, and transactional updates across disparate

ParticleDB 1 aims to unify these workloads in a

single engine with a special focus on AI agents and applications. It

offers transactional SQL, a key-value store, vector search, live

analytics, and user-defined functions called Particles . 2 To integrate with existing systems,

clients can connect through a variety of

interfaces , including the Postgres and Redis protocols, as well as

its own gRPC and HTTP2 APIs. Written from the ground up in Rust,

ParticleDB claims to be orders of magnitude faster than Postgres while preserving the

support their workflow orchestration platform, Conductor .

Conductor was initially built to store data in Redis and Postgres, but

to improve performance, Orkes opted to write their own database.

ParticleDB 1.0.0 offered a limited feature set specifically for

Conductor’s queries, and was deployed as the backing database for some

of their Conductor clusters. A few Orkes customers followed suit. In

preparation for a broader release, Orkes undertook a major refactoring

of ParticleDB, adding a custom wire protocol, more datatypes, additional

OLAP queries, and more. While Orkes and their customers continued to run

1.0.0, they soft launched the refactored versions on particledb.ai . Orkes engaged Jepsen to

test these versions of ParticleDB, beginning with 1.1.4.

While ParticleDB could run as a single node, it also offered a

consensus protocol. This replication feature was available only in

enterprise cloud deployments. The builds Orkes provided did not support

replication, so this report covers only single-node behavior.

that ParticleDB was “formally proven” with a TLA+ proof. However, during

our collaboration no TLA+ specification was available. It is unclear

what properties might be proven, or whether they described ParticleDB as

tactics for syncing its Write-Ahead Log (WAL). The sync

mode called fsync on each commit, groupsync

batched multiple transactions into a single fsync , and

nosync skipped fsync altogether. The Transaction

Engine documentation described sync as offering

“stronger durability” than groupsync . On the other hand,

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.summary_ko: YellowKey라는 제로데이 익스플로잇이 물리적 접근으로 Windows 11의 BitLocker를 우회해 암호화된 드라이브에 접근 가능하게 한다. 수 초 내에 보호를 무효화할 수 있다.
items.content_ko: 보안 연구자 Nightmare-Eclipse가 공개한 YellowKey 제로데이 취약점은 물리적 접근만으로 Windows 11 기본 BitLocker 보호를 우회할 수 있다. YellowKey 익스플로잇의 핵심은 커스텀으로 만들어진 FsTx 폴더 사용으로, fstx.dll과 관련된 디렉터리는 Microsoft의 transactional NTFS 기술을 활용한다.

items.title: Firm that lets you rent out your idle Mac for AI inference workloads warns of plummeting token costs — Darkbloom network sees earnings drop to $1.23 a day as Anthropic tokens fall 77%.
items.content:
Darkbloom, a decentralized AI inference network that aggregates and sells spare compute capacity from Macs, told its members to expect revenues to fall as token prices continue to drop. According to The Register , the price per million tokens for Anthropic dropped by 77% in under five months, falling to $0.62 in October 2026 from $2.65 in May.

AI data centers are swallowing the world's memory and storage supply

Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible

Chip scarcity assaults auto industry amid the worsening Nexperia and DRAM crisis

“Data centers have become cheaper. Output per NVIDIA cluster is up ~20x this year, and their margins are wide enough to cut prices 90 percent and still profit at 50 percent,” said Kydo, a researcher from Eigen Labs, the developer of the compute platform. “The market caught up to our price. We could go lower, but then most of you would earn even less [than] nothing.”

It’s estimated that someone running an M5 Pro Mac Mini with 64GB of Unified Memory could earn as much as $192 per month. This is the best-case scenario, though; the median earnings of the top 50 operators on Darkbloom’s leaderboard are about $159.86 per month. This translates to about $5.26 daily or $1,918.50 annually. However, if we account for Anthropic’s 77% token price drop, earnings will fall to a measly $36.77 per month, or about $1.23 per day.

AI token prices are falling so fast that they've even outpaced Moore’s Law , with some reports saying AI is becoming 50% cheaper every quarter and up to 13 times more affordable every year. News of companies blowing through their annual AI budgets in months has less to do with per-token price and more with the number of tokens, as agentic AI use outpaces token price drops. Aside from that, OpenRouter, Darkbloom’s primary client, has started prioritizing decode speed, quantization, and prefill speed, putting users without a top-of-the-line Max or Ultra Apple chip at a disadvantage.

Despite that, Darkbloom says it will not sit idly by and let some users lose out because of these changes. The network is analyzing model demand to advise members on which models are in higher demand right now. It’s also looking at other kinds of workload beyond inference, including distributed CI/CD jobs, improving network performance to better compete against other computer providers/aggregators, and finding other clients outside of OpenRouter.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.
